source.title: Identifying Legal Holdings with LLMs: A Systematic Study of Performance, Scale, and Memorization

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present. Figure 5's plotted values are not available in the extracted text.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates downstream benchmark performance across model sizes, using CaseHOLD macro F1 rather than held-out pretraining loss or compute-optimal training experiments.
record.gate_note: Rows record the study's CaseHOLD evaluations across models and its citation-anonymization evaluation. The text also reports answer-match rates and accuracy grouped by the number of unique model answers, but these do not test the claim versions. Previously published results cited for comparison are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures zero-shot CaseHOLD macro F1 for 8 models in three families (Llama 3.2, Amazon Nova, GPT-4o) and reports that performance rises with model size within each family. This is a new downstream legal-task setting bearing on V6. It is a weak test: there is no fitted curve, no compute or token axis, and parameter counts are stated only for Llama. It is T3 rather than T2 because it applies the downstream-scaling question to a new domain benchmark and does not use a different method on loss scaling.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that CaseHOLD performance scales with model size across three families, and that general-purpose LLMs zero-shot match or beat custom legal models. They add that performance survives citation anonymization (0.744 to 0.728 F1), suggesting it is not mere case-name memorization.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates zero-shot downstream benchmark performance with macro F1, rather than fitting held-out pretraining loss scaling laws or measuring compute-optimal training allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Model family and size; citation anonymization changes the reported benchmark results.

fits_no_version.finding: Macro F1 drops from 0.744 to 0.728 after citation anonymization, and 88% of answers are unchanged.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: CaseHOLD performance of LLMs is largely robust to anonymizing case names and citations, suggesting limited reliance on memorization.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Law (ICAIL 2025)
record.problems: Figure 5's individual plotted scores are unavailable in the extracted text, and the text reports no uncertainty estimates. The study evaluates one benchmark; it does not fit scaling laws or quantify compute, token counts, or the model sizes for several families. The GPT4o score is inconsistent in the paper's text (0.744 versus 0.742).
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant model evaluations were left out. Figure 5 scores unavailable in the extracted text are represented as figure-only rows.

untested.parts: Whether improvement is predictable in functional form (no fit, no extrapolation). No relation to pretraining loss or compute. Only one benchmark. Parameter counts are not disclosed for the Nova and GPT-4o families.
Not tested: no pretraining loss is measured.
Not tested: no fitted law is used to predict larger runs.
Not tested: no compute-optimal allocation is examined.
Not tested: no shape variation at fixed parameter count.
Not tested: no other modalities or training regimes.
Not tested: no fitting choices are examined.

missing.what: Per-model macro F1 values for six of the eight models, needed to judge the size of within-family gains.

record.verdict_notes: The evidence for V6 is thin. There are only 2–3 points per family, scores are figure-only for most models, there are no uncertainty estimates, and sizes are undisclosed for the proprietary families. The cross-family size gap also confounds parameters with other differences, such as the vision variants in Llama 3.2 11B/90B. A researcher should treat this as qualitative support for 'bigger is better' on a legal benchmark, not as evidence of predictable scaling.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling with parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power-law fits on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities and training regimes, including repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer.
The study tests performance across model size on one downstream benchmark; it does not test performance against pretraining loss or across other downstream tasks.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup or fitting choices, and departures from single power laws.

relationships.condition: Zero-shot CaseHOLD with a chain-of-thought prompt, within the Llama 3.2 (3B/11B/90B), Amazon Nova (Micro/Lite/Pro) and GPT-4o (mini/full) families
relationships.reason: The authors state macro F1 improves with size in every family (Fig. 5; r1–r8). This shows monotone ordering only: Nova and GPT sizes are inferred from tier names, and no curve is fitted.
relationships.display_finding: Macro F1 increased with model size or tier in every family, although Nova and GPT sizes were inferred from tier names.
